metrics.note: NEEDS_REVIEW treated as predicted positive (conservative) for precision/recall calculation

per_finding.gt_notes: Direct string concatenation of userId into SELECT — classic SQL injection sink
per_finding.ai_reasoning: User-controlled userId is concatenated directly into a SQL SELECT statement without parameterization. This is a confirmed SQL injection sink.

per_finding.gt_notes: Template literal interpolation of name into SQL string — user-controlled input reaches query
per_finding.ai_reasoning: Template literal interpolation embeds the name parameter directly into the SQL string. Parameterized queries or an ORM are required.

per_finding.gt_notes: req.query passed directly to MongoDB find() — allows operator injection e.g. {$gt:''}
per_finding.ai_reasoning: Passing the entire req.query object to MongoDB find() allows an attacker to inject query operators like {$gt:''} to bypass authentication or exfiltrate data.

per_finding.gt_notes: req.body passed directly to findOne() — auth bypass via {$ne:null} is trivial
per_finding.ai_reasoning: req.body passed to findOne() enables NoSQL operator injection. An attacker can send {username:{$ne:null}, password:{$ne:null}} to bypass authentication.

per_finding.gt_notes: Unsanitized userInput assigned to innerHTML — classic stored/reflected XSS sink
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The variable userInput is assigned directly to innerHTML without any sanitization. An attacker-supplied script tag would execute in the victim's browser.

per_finding.gt_notes: req.params.filename used directly in fs.readFile — ../../etc/passwd traversal possible
per_finding.ai_reasoning: req.params.filename flows into fs.readFile without path normalization or allowlist validation. A path like ../../etc/passwd would succeed.

per_finding.gt_notes: Scanner fired on the comment line containing 'eval()' — not executable code
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The matched line is a code comment ('// TP-07: eval() with external input'), not an actual eval() call. The real finding is on line 59.

per_finding.gt_notes: eval(expression) with externally supplied expression — arbitrary code execution
per_finding.ai_reasoning: eval() is called with an expression parameter that originates from external input. This allows arbitrary JavaScript execution in the process context.

per_finding.gt_notes: Scanner matched 'child_process.*exec' against a comment line — not executable code
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The evidence string starts with '//' indicating this is a comment line. The actual cp.exec() call on line 64 uses an aliased require ('cp') which the rule does not catch.

per_finding.gt_notes: jwt.decode() does not verify the signature — attacker can forge any token payload
per_finding.ai_reasoning: jwt.decode() is used instead of jwt.verify(). This skips cryptographic signature verification, allowing an attacker to forge any payload without knowing the secret.

per_finding.gt_notes: jwt.verify(token, null) disables signature verification — equivalent to jwt.decode()
per_finding.ai_reasoning: Passing null as the secret to jwt.verify() disables HMAC signature checking entirely. The function accepts any token regardless of signature validity.

per_finding.gt_notes: MD5 used to hash passwords — broken for this use case, rainbow tables exist
per_finding.ai_reasoning: MD5 is used to hash passwords. It is cryptographically broken for this purpose — rainbow tables and GPU cracking make MD5 password hashes trivial to reverse. Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2.

per_finding.gt_notes: Scanner fired on a comment line mentioning 'token' and 'Math.random()' — not code
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The evidence is a comment line ('// TP-12: Math.random() used as auth session token'). The actual vulnerable code is on line 91.

per_finding.gt_notes: Math.random() used as session token — predictable, not cryptographically secure
per_finding.ai_reasoning: Math.random() produces a 64-bit float with only ~53 bits of entropy and is not a CSPRNG. Session tokens must use crypto.randomBytes() or crypto.randomUUID() to be unpredictable.

per_finding.gt_notes: Object.assign onto existing object with req.body — __proto__ key injection possible
per_finding.ai_reasoning: Object.assign merges req.body into an existing object. An attacker can supply {__proto__:{isAdmin:true}} to pollute Object.prototype and escalate privileges application-wide.

per_finding.gt_notes: cors({ origin: '*' }) allows any domain to make cross-origin requests with credentials
per_finding.ai_reasoning: A wildcard CORS origin allows any external domain to make cross-origin requests. If combined with credentials (cookies/auth headers), this enables cross-site request attacks.

per_finding.gt_notes: Hardcoded demo API key in source — still a real secret-management finding because credentials are embedded in code and git history
per_finding.ai_reasoning: A hardcoded API key is embedded directly in source code. Even if it is a demo credential, this is the exact secret-management pattern the rule is meant to catch because real deployments often leak keys this way.

per_finding.gt_notes: user.password logged to console — appears in log aggregation systems (CloudWatch, Splunk)
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The console.log call includes user.password in a debug function. Without evidence this runs in production environments, this may be intentional development-time debugging rather than a production logging leak.

per_finding.gt_notes: innerHTML receives output of escapeHtml() — sanitized before assignment, not exploitable
per_finding.ai_reasoning: innerHTML is assigned the output of escapeHtml(). If this function properly encodes HTML special characters the risk is mitigated, but the implementation is not visible in this file.

per_finding.gt_notes: SHA-1 used for content-addressed cache key, not for auth/signing — collision attacks do not apply here
per_finding.ai_reasoning: SHA-1 is used to generate a cache key from file content. SHA-1 collision attacks affect digital signatures and certificates, not content-addressed lookups where collision resistance is irrelevant.

per_finding.gt_notes: Scanner fired on a comment line that mentions 'key' and 'Math.random()' — not code
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The evidence line begins with '//' — this is a comment describing the intent, not executable code. The rule matched the word 'key' inside the identifier 'cacheKey' in the comment text.

per_finding.gt_notes: cacheKey matched 'key' substring — this is a transient UI deduplication id, not a cryptographic secret
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The rule matched 'key' inside the variable name 'cacheKey'. The value is used as a transient UI element id for grid deduplication — unpredictability is not a security requirement here.

per_finding.gt_notes: Scanner fired on comment text '127.0.0.1 is localhost' — not a hardcoded production endpoint
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The matched line is a comment explaining that 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The regex fired on an inline comment rather than an actual assignment.

per_finding.gt_notes: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address — not a production secret; used only in local dev config
per_finding.ai_reasoning: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address (localhost). Hardcoding a local dev DB host is standard practice and does not expose production infrastructure.

per_finding.gt_notes: Value 'Change_Me_On_First_Login!' is an explicit placeholder — not a real credential
per_finding.ai_reasoning: The value 'Change_Me_On_First_Login!' appears to be a documentation placeholder rather than a real credential. However, if the application falls back to this value when no env var is set, it remains a real risk.
